summary: Brazil is the largest country in South America by area and population, has the Amazon rainforest, was formerly a Portuguese colony, and is known for football, Carnival and its diverse ethnic cultures.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived when the Portuguese navigator Cabral reached Brazil in 1500; in 1549 Jesuit missionaries began preaching to the indigenous people in Bahia. During the colonial period Catholicism was the only legal religion, and it remained the state religion after independence in 1822, until the republic was founded in 1889 and the 1891 constitution separated church and state. Brazil was long the country with the most Catholics in the world, but the proportion has fallen from over 90% in 1970 to about 50-odd percent.

ranking.name: Evangelicalism / Protestantism
ranking.description: Evangelicalism and Protestantism arrived in the 19th century with German immigrants and American missionaries; in the 1910s Swedish-born missionaries founded the Assemblies of God in Pará, the starting point of Pentecostalism in Brazil. From the 1970s, Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal churches (such as the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, founded in 1977) grew rapidly in the poor neighborhoods on the urban periphery and took an active part in politics, and the proportion of Evangelicals has risen to more than a quarter.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has continued to grow in recent decades, concentrated in big cities such as Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo and among younger generations. The spread of education, urbanization and alienation from the churches are the main reasons, but most non-religious people still believe in God and simply do not belong to any church.

ranking.name: Spiritism
ranking.description: Spiritism was founded in the 1850s by the French educator Allan Kardec and, after reaching Brazil in the late 19th century, became widely popular among the middle class. The Brazilian medium Chico Xavier (1910–2002) published hundreds of 'psychographed' books, making Brazil the country with the most Spiritists in the world, known for its charitable hospitals and social services.

ranking.name: Afro-Brazilian religions
ranking.description: Afro-Brazilian religions include Candomblé and Umbanda, originating from the roughly four million African slaves trafficked to Brazil during the colonial period, especially the orisha faith of the Yoruba. To evade prohibitions, the slaves matched African deities to Catholic saints, forming religious syncretism. Candomblé is centered on the state of Bahia, and although self-identified adherents are only about 1%, its cultural influence extends across music, food and festivals.

religion.background: Before the Portuguese arrived in 1500, the indigenous peoples of Brazil had diverse shamanic and nature beliefs. During the colonial period Catholicism was the state religion, and orders such as the Jesuits preached to the indigenous people, while the beliefs brought by roughly four million African slaves blended with Catholicism, forming religions such as Candomblé. Brazil became a republic in 1889, and the 1891 constitution separated church and state, and religious freedom allowed Protestantism, Spiritism and others to develop. From the late 20th century, Pentecostalism has grown rapidly and the proportion of Catholics has kept falling, making Brazil one of the countries with the most dramatic religious change.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese arrived with Portuguese colonization in 1500; in the early colonial period the indigenous Tupi language was the coastal lingua franca, and Jesuit missionaries also developed the 'Língua Geral' based on Tupi. In 1758 the Portuguese prime minister, the Marquis of Pombal, ordered a ban on the use of the Língua Geral and forcibly promoted Portuguese. In the 19th and 20th centuries, large numbers of Italian, German and Japanese immigrants switched to speaking Portuguese from the second generation on, making it the mother tongue of about 98% of the population, and Brazil the country with the most Portuguese speakers in the world.

ranking.name: German dialects (Hunsrückisch and others)
ranking.description: German dialects were brought mainly by German immigrants who moved to the south from the 19th century; in 1824 the first German immigrants settled in São Leopoldo in Rio Grande do Sul. Hunsrückisch originates from the dialects of Germany's Rhineland region and is still used in some towns of Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina in the south. During the Second World War the Vargas government banned the public use of German, greatly reducing its speakers.

language.history: When the Portuguese reached Brazil in 1500, there were hundreds of indigenous languages there. In the early colonial period, the 'Língua Geral' based on Tupi was the common language among colonists, missionaries and indigenous people, until the Marquis of Pombal ordered the promotion of Portuguese in 1758. Brazilian Portuguese absorbed many words from Tupi (such as abacaxi, pineapple) and from African languages (such as samba). European and Japanese immigrants of the late 19th and early 20th centuries brought many languages, but the nationalization policy of the Vargas government in the 1930s–40s forcibly promoted Portuguese-language education, making Brazil a highly linguistically unified country.

ranking.name: Feijoada
ranking.description: Black beans are stewed for a long time with pork, sausage, pig's ears, pig's feet and dried beef, and eaten with rice, sautéed collard greens, orange slices and farofa (manioc flour).
ranking.history: Feijoada is often said to be a dish slaves made from the pig's ears, feet and other parts their masters discarded, but historians point out that this claim lacks evidence; it more likely derives from the Portuguese bean-and-meat stew tradition and took shape in the restaurants of 19th-century Rio de Janeiro. In the 20th century it became the national dish of Brazil, traditionally eaten at midday on Wednesdays or Saturdays, accompanied by the caipirinha cocktail.

ranking.name: Pão de queijo (cheese bread)
ranking.description: Manioc starch, eggs, milk and Minas cheese are kneaded into small balls and baked, with a crisp crust, a chewy interior and a rich cheese aroma.
ranking.history: Pão de queijo originates from the state of Minas Gerais; it is said that during the 18th-century gold rush, slaves on local farms used manioc starch in place of expensive wheat flour to make bread, adding cheese from the local farms. Manioc is a traditional indigenous crop, while cheese is a dairy culture brought by the Portuguese colonists. From the mid-20th century it spread from Minas Gerais across the country, and today it is the most common snack at Brazilian breakfasts and afternoon teas.

ranking.name: Churrasco
ranking.description: Large cuts of beef are seasoned with coarse salt, skewered on long iron spits and slowly grilled over charcoal; waiters bring the whole skewer to the table to carve, and it can be eaten all-you-can-eat.
ranking.history: Churrasco originates from the gaucho herders of Rio Grande do Sul in the south in the 19th century, who grazed cattle on the pampas and grilled beef over charcoal fires in the open. In the 1940s–60s, immigrants from southern Brazil opened 'churrascaria' restaurants in São Paulo and elsewhere, developing the all-you-can-eat 'rodízio' format in which waiters bring meat to the table to carve. Today it represents Brazilian weekend gatherings and celebrations.

ranking.name: Moqueca
ranking.description: A seafood stew of fish or shrimp with onion, tomato, bell pepper and cilantro, simmered in a clay pot with coconut milk and palm oil, brightly colored.
ranking.history: Moqueca has two main versions: the Bahian version adds palm oil (dendê) and coconut milk, reflecting the deep influence of African slaves on Bahian cuisine; the Espírito Santo version does not use palm oil and is cooked in the traditional indigenous clay pot, which locals stress is the older way. The two states still argue over which is authentic, and it is regarded as a representative dish of Brazil's blend of indigenous, African and Portuguese cultures.

ranking.name: Brigadeiro
ranking.description: Condensed milk, cocoa powder and butter are cooked into a thick chocolate paste, rolled into small balls and coated in chocolate sprinkles, with a soft, chewy, sweet texture.
ranking.history: The brigadeiro was born in the 1940s and is linked to Brigadier Eduardo Gomes, a candidate in Brazil's 1945 presidential election: his supporters made and sold this sweet to raise funds for him and named it after his military rank, 'brigadeiro' (brigadier). During the Second World War, milk and sugar were in short supply and condensed milk became a convenient substitute. Today it is indispensable at every Brazilian birthday party and is regarded as Brazil's national sweet.
